claim: PINK1 and parkin mutations lead to autosomal recessive forms of Parkinson's disease
source: Mutations in PINK1, a mitochondria-localized serine–threonine kinase, and Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, lead to autosomal recessive forms of the disease (Kitada et al., 1998; Valente et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kitada et al., 1998; Valente et al., 2004)

claim: PINK1 and parkin act in the same genetic pathway in Drosophila
source: Genetic studies in Drosophila first demonstrated that PINK1 and parkin act in the same genetic pathway, with PINK1 positively regulating parkin, to regulate mitochondrial integrity and function (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006)

claim: Mitochondrial morphology is maintained by a balance between mitochondrial fusion promoted by mitofusin and mitochondrial fission controlled by Drp1
source: Mitochondrial morphology is maintained by a balance between two opposing actions, mitochondrial fusion that is promoted by mitofusin (mfn) and mitochondrial fission that is controlled by Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) (Chan, 2012; Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Chan, 2012; Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012)

claim: Downregulation of mfn or overexpression of drp1 suppresses multiple phenotypes associated with lack of PINK1 or parkin in Drosophila
source: Genetic studies in Drosophila have shown that downregulation of mfn or overexpression of drp1 suppresses multiple phenotypes associated with lack of PINK1 or parkin, including defects in mitochondrial integrity, cell death, tissue health, and flight ability (Deng et al., 2008; Poole et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Deng et al., 2008; Poole et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008)

claim: Parkin ubiquitinates Mfn and promotes Mfn degradation
source: Parkin ubiquitinates Mfn and promotes Mfn degradation (Poole et al., 2010; Ziviani et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Poole et al., 2010; Ziviani et al., 2010)

claim: The PINK1/Parkin pathway promotes mitophagy in mammalian cells
source: In addition to mitochondrial dynamics, the PINK1/Parkin pathway promotes mitophagy, selective autophagic degradation of defective mitochondria in mammalian cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the PINK1/Parkin pathway

claim: Loss of mitochondrial membrane potential leads to recruitment of Parkin to depolarized mitochondria, resulting in autophagic degradation
source: Accumulation of mitochondrial damage can result in loss of mitochondrial membrane potential. This leads to recruitment of Parkin to the depolarized mitochondria, ultimately resulting in autophagic degradation of these mitochondria (Narendra et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2010; Gegg et al., 2010; Geisler et al., 2010; Matsuda et al., 2010; Narendra et al., 2010; Okatsu et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2010; Vives-Bauza et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Narendra et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2010; Gegg et al., 2010; Geisler et al., 2010; Matsuda et al., 2010; Narendra et al., 2010; Okatsu et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2010; Vives-Bauza et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011)

claim: Parkin-mediated mitophagy occurs in mouse cortical neurons and heart muscle
source: Parkin-mediated mitophagy also occurs in mouse cortical neurons and heart muscle (Cai et al., 2012; Chen and Dorn, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Cai et al., 2012; Chen and Dorn, 2013)

claim: Parkin-dependent ubiquitination of Mfn is followed by proteasome-dependent degradation during mitophagy
source: An important step during this process is Parkin-dependent ubiquitination of Mfn and other substrates, followed by their proteasome-dependent degradation (Tanaka et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Tanaka et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011)

claim: PINK1 and parkin mutant fibroblasts from PD patients show deregulation of mitochondrial dynamics and modest defects in mitochondrial clearance
source: Relevant to PD, PINK1 and parkin mutant fibroblasts from PD patients also show deregulation of mitochondrial dynamics and modest defects in the clearance of mitochondria (Rakovic et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Rakovic et al., 2011, 2013)

claim: Mice lacking PINK1 or parkin bear only subtle phenotypes related to dopaminergic neuronal degeneration or mitochondrial morphology change
source: An important puzzle in the field of PD research is why mice lacking PINK1 or parkin bear only subtle phenotypes related to dopaminergic neuronal degeneration or mitochondrial morphology change (Palacino et al., 2004; Perez and Palmiter, 2005; Perez et al., 2005; Kitada et al., 2007; Frank-Cannon et al., 2008; Gautier et al., 2008; Gispert et al., 2009; Kitada et al., 2009; Akundi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Palacino et al., 2004; Perez and Palmiter, 2005; Perez et al., 2005; Kitada et al., 2007; Frank-Cannon et al., 2008; Gautier et al., 2008; Gispert et al., 2009; Kitada et al., 2009; Akundi et al., 2011)

claim: Knockdown of parkin in adult dopaminergic neurons results in more striking neuronal degeneration than developmental knockout
source: Indeed, when parkin is knocked down in adult dopaminergic neurons rather than during development, more striking neuronal degeneration is observed (Dawson et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Dawson et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012)

claim: MUL1 has SUMO ligase activity that stabilizes Drp1 in mammalian systems
source: Work in mammalian systems shows that MUL1 has small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) ligase activity, stabilizing Drp1 (Harder et al., 2004; Braschi et al., 2009), or ubiquitin ligase activity, degrading Mfn (Lokireddy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Harder et al., 2004; Braschi et al., 2009)

claim: MUL1 has ubiquitin ligase activity that degrades Mfn in mammalian systems
source: Work in mammalian systems shows that MUL1 has small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) ligase activity, stabilizing Drp1 (Harder et al., 2004; Braschi et al., 2009), or ubiquitin ligase activity, degrading Mfn (Lokireddy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Lokireddy et al., 2012)

claim: MUL1 expression in mammalian cells results in smaller and more fragmented mitochondria
source: As expected from a protein with these proposed biochemical activities, MUL1 expression in mammalian cells results in smaller and more fragmented mitochondria (Li et al., 2008; Neuspiel, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Li et al., 2008; Neuspiel, 2008)

claim: MUL1 suppresses PINK1 or parkin mutant phenotypes in Drosophila
source: In this study, we show that MUL1 suppresses PINK1 or parkin mutant phenotypes in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: MUL1 suppression of PINK1/parkin mutant phenotypes is achieved through ubiquitin-dependent degradation of Mitofusin
source: The suppression is achieved through the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of Mitofusin, which itself causes PINK1/parkin mutant-like toxicity when overexpressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Overexpression of Mitofusin causes PINK1/parkin mutant-like toxicity
source: The suppression is achieved through the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of Mitofusin, which itself causes PINK1/parkin mutant-like toxicity when overexpressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Removing MUL1 in PINK1 or parkin loss-of-function mutants aggravates phenotypes and leads to lethality in flies
source: We further show that removing MUL1 in PINK1 or parkin loss-of-function mutant aggravates phenotypes caused by loss of either gene alone, leading to lethality in flies and degeneration in mouse cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Removing MUL1 in PINK1 or parkin loss-of-function mutants causes degeneration in mouse cortical neurons
source: We further show that removing MUL1 in PINK1 or parkin loss-of-function mutant aggravates phenotypes caused by loss of either gene alone, leading to lethality in flies and degeneration in mouse cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: MUL1 acts in parallel to the PINK1/parkin pathway on a shared target mitofusin to maintain mitochondrial integrity
source: Together, these observations show that MUL1 acts in parallel to the PINK1/parkin pathway on a shared target mitofusin to maintain mitochondrial integrity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing genetic interactions and shared targets

claim: The MUL1 pathway compensates for loss of PINK1/parkin in both Drosophila and mammals
source: The MUL1 pathway compensates for loss of PINK1/parkin in both Drosophila and mammals and is a promising therapeutic target for PD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from both Drosophila and mammalian systems presented in the manuscript

claim: MUL1 is a promising therapeutic target for Parkinson's disease
source: The MUL1 pathway compensates for loss of PINK1/parkin in both Drosophila and mammals and is a promising therapeutic target for PD.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the experimental findings about MUL1's compensatory role

claim: Drosophila MUL1 has 52% amino acid similarity to human MUL1
source: Drosophila MUL1 (CG1134) encodes a protein with a similar domain structure, and 52% amino acid similarity to human MUL1 (Figure 1A,B).

evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1C' and cited research (Park et al., 2006)

claim: MUL1 does not affect Parkin recruitment to mitochondria in wild-type HeLa cells after antimycin A treatment
source: In wild-type, without antimycin A treatment, Parkin mainly localizes in the cytosol (Figure 7A). However, following antimycin A treatment for 3 hrs, most Parkin was translocated to the mitochondria (Figure 7B,D). After 24 hrs of antimycin A treatment, Parkin was found dispersed in the cytosol and mitochondria were no longer observed, indicating that mitophagy had occurred (Figure 7C,E). To ensure there was no delay in mitophagy, we also assayed cells that were treated with antimycin A for 6, 12, 16 and 20 hrs (Figure 7F, data not shown). In all cells, mitophagy was observed at least 16 hrs after antimycin A treatment. No significant differences were observed in the fraction of Parkin recruited to mitochondria, or the fraction of mitochondria that underwent mitophagy, at any of these time points, for wild-type and MUL1 knockout cells (Figure 7B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-F

claim: MUL1 does not affect mitophagy in wild-type HeLa cells after antimycin A treatment
source: In wild-type, without antimycin A treatment, Parkin mainly localizes in the cytosol (Figure 7A). However, following antimycin A treatment for 3 hrs, most Parkin was translocated to the mitochondria (Figure 7B,D). After 24 hrs of antimycin A treatment, Parkin was found dispersed in the cytosol and mitochondria were no longer observed, indicating that mitophagy had occurred (Figure 7C,E). To ensure there was no delay in mitophagy, we also assayed cells that were treated with antimycin A for 6, 12, 16 and 20 hrs (Figure 7F, data not shown). In all cells, mitophagy was observed at least 16 hrs after antimycin A treatment. No significant differences were observed in the fraction of Parkin recruited to mitochondria, or the fraction of mitochondria that underwent mitophagy, at any of these time points, for wild-type and MUL1 knockout cells (Figure 7B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-F

claim: PINK1 knockout HeLa cells show almost no Parkin localization to mitochondria and lack of mitophagy
source: As a control, PINK1 knockout HeLa cells showed almost no Parkin localization to mitochondria and lack of mitophagy (Figure 7B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 7B-F

claim: MUL1 overexpression does not affect Parkin translocation to mitochondria
source: Finally, MUL1 overexpression also had no effect on Parkin translocation (Figure 7G–H) and did not block mitophagy (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 7G-H

claim: MUL1 overexpression does not block mitophagy
source: Finally, MUL1 overexpression also had no effect on Parkin translocation (Figure 7G–H) and did not block mitophagy (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data not shown in the manuscript

claim: Neither loss of MUL1 nor its overexpression alters Parkin translocation or mitophagy
source: Thus, neither loss of MUL1 nor its overexpression altered Parkin translocation or mitophagy. These results are consistent with MUL1 acting in parallel to PINK1/parkin in Drosophila, and suggest that MUL1 regulates mitochondrial health through a distinct pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on Parkin translocation and mitophagy

claim: MUL1 regulates mitochondrial health through a pathway distinct from PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy
source: Thus, neither loss of MUL1 nor its overexpression altered Parkin translocation or mitophagy. These results are consistent with MUL1 acting in parallel to PINK1/parkin in Drosophila, and suggest that MUL1 regulates mitochondrial health through a distinct pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of MUL1 on mitophagy combined with its effects on mitochondrial morphology

claim: GFP-MUL1 localizes to mitochondria in cell bodies and axons of primary cortical neurons
source: GFP-MUL1 localizes to the mitochondria in cell bodies and axons of the primary cortical neurons (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: parkin knockout neurons with MUL1 knockdown show reduced TMRE intensity indicating decreased mitochondrial membrane potential
source: In contrast to other neurons, parkin knockout neurons with MUL1 knockdown show reduced TMRE intensity (F and F′), indicating decreased Δψm. Scale bars: 10 µm. (G) Quantification of relative TMRE intensity.
evidence: The claim is supported by TMRE staining and quantification data shown in Figure 8F-F', G

claim: MUL1 knockdown in parkin KO neurons results in enhanced fragmentation of neurites
source: MUL1 knockdown in parkin KO neurons results in enhanced fragmentation of neurites. Representative wild-type (H and I) and parkin KO (J–K″) cortical neurons transfected with scrambled or MUL1 shRNA and labeled with GFP (confirming transfection of shRNA and labeling axons and dendrites).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 8H-M

claim: MUL1 knockdown in parkin KO neurons results in dendritic retraction
source: Quantitative analysis showing enhanced process fragmentation (L) and dendritic retraction (M).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 8M

claim: MUL1 knockdown in wild-type neurons results in a minor increase in dendritic retraction but no significant process fragmentation
source: MUL1 knockdown in cells from wild-type mice resulted in a minor increase in dendritic retraction but no significant process fragmentation as compared with wild-type cells (Figure 8H,L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 8H, L, M

claim: Cortical neurons from parkin KO mice show slightly increased process fragmentation but no dendritic retraction
source: Cortical neurons from parkin KO mice showed slightly increased process fragmentation but no dendritic retraction (Figure 8J,L,M), as compared with wild-type cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 8J, L, M

claim: MUL1 knockdown in parkin KO neurons results in a dramatic increase in neurons with dendritic and axonal fragmentation and retraction
source: In contrast, MUL1 knockdown in parkin KO neurons resulted in a dramatic increase in the number of neurons with dendritic and axonal fragmentation and retraction (Figure 8K–K″,L–M; process fragmentation: total number of neurons examined: n > 115 and n > 127 each genotype for fragmentation and dendritic retraction analysis, respectively), indicative of early neurodegeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 8K-K'', L-M

claim: MUL1 acts in parallel to the PINK1/parkin pathway to ensure mitochondrial integrity and function in primary cortical neurons
source: These observations suggest that MUL1 acts in parallel to the PINK1/parkin pathway to ensure mitochondrial integrity and function, thus maintaining neuronal health in primary cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enhanced phenotypes in parkin KO neurons with MUL1 knockdown

claim: MUL1 does not act on PINK1 or parkin
source: The mechanism of this suppression is unique in that MUL1 does not act on PINK1 or parkin, nor does it function as a downstream target.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data showing MUL1 acts in parallel to PINK1/parkin

claim: MUL1 does not function as a downstream target of PINK1/parkin
source: The mechanism of this suppression is unique in that MUL1 does not act on PINK1 or parkin, nor does it function as a downstream target.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data showing MUL1 acts in parallel to PINK1/parkin

claim: mfn is crucial for actions downstream of PINK1/parkin to maintain mitochondrial function and tissue health
source: mfn is crucial for actions downstream of PINK1/parkin to maintain mitochondrial function and tissue health (Figure 9B), as overexpression of mfn leads to pathology similar to lack of PINK1/parkin function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mfn overexpression phenocopies PINK1/parkin mutants

claim: The increase in Mfn level needs to reach a threshold for overt muscle cell degeneration to occur
source: We hypothesize that the increase in the Mfn level needs to reach a threshold, such as that observed in the PINK1/parkin mutant backgrounds, but not in the MUL1 null background, in order for overt muscle cell degeneration to occur (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that MUL1 null alone does not cause severe phenotypes

claim: MUL1 physically binds to Mfn
source: Biochemically, MUL1 binds to Mfn, and loss of MUL1 results in decreased ubiquitination of Mfn and increased Mfn levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data

claim: Loss of MUL1 results in decreased ubiquitination of Mfn
source: Biochemically, MUL1 binds to Mfn, and loss of MUL1 results in decreased ubiquitination of Mfn and increased Mfn levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data

claim: MUL1 may directly ubiquitinate Mfn leading to its degradation
source: These observations suggest that MUL1 may directly ubiquitinate Mfn, leading to its degradation (Figure 9A). Alternatively, MUL1 may act via an intermediary that promotes Mfn ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the biochemical data showing MUL1 binds Mfn and affects its ubiquitination

claim: MUL1 may act via an intermediary that promotes Mfn ubiquitination and degradation
source: These observations suggest that MUL1 may directly ubiquitinate Mfn, leading to its degradation (Figure 9A). Alternatively, MUL1 may act via an intermediary that promotes Mfn ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, presenting an alternative mechanism

claim: Overexpression of MUL1 almost completely suppresses all aspects of PINK1/parkin null phenotypes in Drosophila
source: In Drosophila, overexpression of MUL1 almost completely suppresses all aspects of the PINK1/parkin null phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data showing rescue of various phenotypes

claim: Treatments that manipulate MUL1 expression or activity may have potential as therapeutic strategies
source: Thus, treatments that manipulate MUL1 expression or activity may have potential as therapeutics strategies.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the therapeutic implications of the findings

claim: Compensation by MUL1 may contribute to the subtle phenotypes in PINK1 or parkin mutant mice
source: Our studies provide genetic and cellular clues that suggest compensation by MUL1 may contribute to the subtle phenotypes in PINK1 or parkin mutant mice.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the compensatory role of MUL1 observed in the study

claim: Upregulating MUL1 may rescue the pathology due to lack of PINK1 or PARKIN
source: Regarding PD therapies, optimizing the function of MUL1 is likely to be beneficial for PINK1/PARKIN patients; upregulating MUL1 may rescue the pathology due to lack of PINK1 or PARKIN.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the therapeutic implications of the findings

claim: Downregulating MUL1 or mutations in MUL1 may lead to disruption of the compensatory pathway and accelerated disease progression
source: In contrast, downregulating MUL1 and/or mutations in MUL1 may lead to disruption of this compensatory pathway in maintaining mitochondrial integrity and function, and result in accelerated disease progression.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the compensatory role of MUL1

claim: Mfn is localized to the mitochondrial outer membrane
source: Mfn is localized to the mitochondrial outer membrane (OM) (Figure 9A) and is a key molecule that regulates mitochondrial fusion in response to various cellular processes.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Mfn localization

claim: Mfn is a key molecule that regulates mitochondrial fusion in response to various cellular processes
source: Mfn is localized to the mitochondrial outer membrane (OM) (Figure 9A) and is a key molecule that regulates mitochondrial fusion in response to various cellular processes.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Mfn function

claim: The level of Mfn is expected to be tightly regulated due to its importance
source: Due to its importance, the level of Mfn is expected to be tightly regulated, and this may require several E3 ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases that respond to different stimuli (Gegg et al., 2010; Park et al., 2010; Leboucher et al., 2012; Lokireddy et al., 2012; Anton et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the importance of Mfn and supported by citations (Gegg et al., 2010; Park et al., 2010; Leboucher et al., 2012; Lokireddy et al., 2012; Anton et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2013)

claim: Parkin translocates to depolarized mitochondria before it degrades Mfn
source: In the case of mitochondrial damage, Parkin translocates to depolarized mitochondria before it degrades Mfn (Figure 9A), thus preventing damaged mitochondria from fusing with healthy ones.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Parkin-mediated mitophagy

claim: MUL1 is anchored on the mitochondrial outer membrane
source: As an E3 ligase anchored on the OM (Li et al., 2008; Figure 9A), MUL1 is constantly present in the vicinity of Mfn, thus mediating Mfn clearance either constitutively or in a regulated manner in response to different stress signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Li et al., 2008) and schematic in Figure 9A

claim: MUL1 is constantly present in the vicinity of Mfn
source: As an E3 ligase anchored on the OM (Li et al., 2008; Figure 9A), MUL1 is constantly present in the vicinity of Mfn, thus mediating Mfn clearance either constitutively or in a regulated manner in response to different stress signals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from MUL1's localization on the mitochondrial outer membrane

claim: MUL1 mediates Mfn clearance either constitutively or in a regulated manner in response to different stress signals
source: As an E3 ligase anchored on the OM (Li et al., 2008; Figure 9A), MUL1 is constantly present in the vicinity of Mfn, thus mediating Mfn clearance either constitutively or in a regulated manner in response to different stress signals.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the mechanism of MUL1 action

claim: Multiple E3 ligases may work in a concerted way to ensure constant Mfn levels
source: It is also possible that multiple E3 ligases work in a concerted way to ensure constant Mfn levels.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the regulation of Mfn levels

claim: CHX treatment leads to stabilization of Mfn levels in HeLa cells lacking MUL1
source: In our study, CHX treatment leads to the stabilization of Mfn levels in HeLa cells lack of MUL1. However, steady-state Mfn levels in these cells are not strongly affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from CHX experiments

claim: Steady-state Mfn levels in HeLa cells lacking MUL1 are not strongly affected
source: In our study, CHX treatment leads to the stabilization of Mfn levels in HeLa cells lack of MUL1. However, steady-state Mfn levels in these cells are not strongly affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data

claim: Other pathways for Mfn regulation may exist including transcriptional feedback, deubiquitinases, and additional E3 ligases
source: This may result from the existence of other pathways for Mfn regulation, such as direct transcriptional feedback regulation on Mfn expression, activities of deubquitinases, and additional E3 ligases.
evidence: The claim is speculative about compensatory mechanisms

claim: MUL1 promotes mitophagy when muscle wasting is stimulated in mice
source: A recent study reports that MUL1 promotes mitophagy, when muscle wasting is stimulated in mice (Lokireddy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Lokireddy et al., 2012)

claim: Overexpression or lack of MUL1 does not affect Parkin-mediated mitophagy induced by mitochondrial damage in HeLa cells
source: Our results show that overexpression or lack of MUL1 does not affect Parkin-mediated mitophagy induced by mitochondrial damage in HeLa cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on Parkin translocation and mitophagy

claim: MUL1 acts in a PINK1/parkin-independent pathway for regulating mitochondrial quality control
source: This further strengthens our hypothesis that MUL1 acts in PINK1/parkin-independent pathway for regulating mitochondrial quality control.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of MUL1 on Parkin-mediated mitophagy

claim: MUL1 forms a complex with VPS35 and VPS26
source: In this regard, it is worth noting that MUL1 forms a complex with VPS35 and VPS26 (Braschi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Braschi et al., 2010)

claim: Mutations in VPS35 have been identified in multiple PD families
source: Since mutations in VPS35 have been identified in multiple PD families (Vilarino-Guell et al., 2011; Zimprich et al., 2011; Kumar et al., 2012; Lesage et al., 2012), it will be particularly interesting to determine if PD-associated mutations in VPS35 have effects on MUL1-dependent degradation of Mfn.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Vilarino-Guell et al., 2011; Zimprich et al., 2011; Kumar et al., 2012; Lesage et al., 2012)

claim: Inhibition of mfn may have important therapeutic potential for PD
source: Finally, our observation that overexpression of mfn alone is sufficient to recapitulate key phenotypes associated with loss of PINK1 or parkin suggests that inhibition of mfn may have important therapeutic potential for PD.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the therapeutic implications of the findings

claim: MUL1 knockdown in wild-type neurons results in increased Mfn2 levels
source: Compared to wild-type neurons transfected with scrambled shRNA, wild-type neurons with MUL1 shRNA, or parkin KO neurons with either scrambled shRNA or MUL1 shRNA had an increased intensity ratio of Mfn2 to Cytochrome C. This suggests that MUL1's role in regulating Mfn2 levels is also conserved in neurons.
